title: Maglev Trains
summary: How maglev trains use magnets to float above a guideway and glide at high speed, where they run today, and why they are hard to build.
poll: Trains that float on magnets are the best way to travel in the future.

versions.title: The Train That Floats
versions.text:
Have you seen a train float? Some trains do! They are maglev trains.

A maglev has no wheels. It floats just above the track. Big magnets lift it up.

Hold two magnets. One way, they pull close. Turn one. Now they push apart. A maglev uses this push to float.

Most trains have wheels. The wheels rub on the track. That rub is friction. It slows the train. It makes noise, too. A maglev does not rub. So it is fast. It is quiet. The ride is smooth.

Magnets in the track make it go. The ones in front pull. The ones in back push. Zoom!

A maglev runs in China. It starts at a big airport. It runs to the city. It goes more than 400 km in an hour. The trip takes 8 minutes.

Japan has a test train. It went 603 km in an hour. No train has gone as fast.

But a maglev costs a lot. It needs its own track. It can not use old tracks.

Saudi Arabia has a fast train. It runs from Makkah to Madinah. It has wheels. One day, we may ride one that floats!

versions.title: The Train That Floats
versions.text:
Can a train float in the air? Some trains can! They are called maglev trains.

A maglev train has no wheels that touch the track. It floats a little bit above it. Strong magnets lift it up.

Have you played with magnets? Hold two of them close. One way, they pull together. Turn one around, and they push apart. A maglev uses this push to float.

A train with wheels rubs on its track. This rubbing is called friction. Friction slows the train down. It makes noise, too. A maglev does not rub on the track. So it can go very fast. It is quiet, and the ride is smooth.

Magnets in the track also move the train. The magnets in front pull the train. The magnets in back push it. Zoom!

A maglev train runs in China. It goes from a big airport to the city of Shanghai. It can go more than 400 km in one hour. The trip takes about 8 minutes.

A test train in Japan went 603 km in one hour. That is the fastest any train has gone.

But a maglev costs a lot to build. It needs its own special track. It can not run on old tracks.

In Saudi Arabia, a fast train links Makkah and Madinah. It runs on wheels. One day, we may ride a train that floats!

versions.title: Maglev: The Floating Train
versions.text:
Imagine riding a train that floats in the air. It sounds like magic. But it is real! These trains are called maglev trains.

A maglev train has no wheels that touch the track. It floats just above a special track. Strong magnets lift it up.

Have you ever played with two magnets? Hold them one way, and they pull close. Turn one, and they push apart. A maglev train uses this push to float.

In Saudi Arabia, a fast train links Makkah and Madinah. It runs on wheels. One day, people may ride trains that float!

versions.title: Maglev: The Floating Train
versions.text:
Imagine riding a train that floats above the ground. It sounds like magic, but it is real. These trains are called maglev trains. The name is short for "magnetic levitation." Levitation means rising up into the air.

A maglev train has no wheels that touch the track. It floats a few centimeters above a special track called a guideway. Strong magnets lift it up.

If you have played with two magnets, you know how they work. Held one way, they pull together. Turn one around, and they push apart. A maglev train uses this push to float.

A normal train has metal wheels that rub on the rails. This rubbing is called friction. It slows a train down and makes noise. A maglev train never touches the guideway, so there is no rubbing. It can go very fast, and the ride is quiet and smooth.

Magnets in the guideway also move the train. The magnets in front of the train pull it. The magnets behind it push it. So the train glides ahead.

One maglev line runs in Shanghai, China. It takes people from the airport to the city at more than 400 kilometers an hour. The trip takes just 8 minutes.

In 2015, a test train in Japan went 603 kilometers an hour. No train has ever gone faster.

But maglev trains cost a lot to build. They need their own guideway. They can not run on old rails.

In Saudi Arabia, a fast train links Makkah and Madinah, but it runs on wheels. One day, people may ride trains that float!

versions.title: Maglev Trains: Riding on Magnets
versions.text:
Imagine a train that floats above the ground as it races along. It sounds like a dream, but it is real. These trains are called maglev trains. The name is short for "magnetic levitation," and levitation means rising into the air.

A maglev train has no wheels touching its track. Instead, it floats between one and ten centimeters above a special track called a guideway. Strong magnets hold it up.

If you have played with two magnets, you already know the secret. Held one way, they pull together. Turn one around, and they push apart. A maglev train uses this pushing force to lift itself off the guideway.

On a regular train, metal wheels roll against metal rails. The rubbing between them is called friction, and it slows the train, makes noise, and wears out the parts. A maglev train never touches the guideway. So there is almost no friction from the track. It can travel very fast, and the ride is quiet and smooth.

Magnets in the guideway also move the train forward. They switch on and off in a pattern. The magnets ahead of the train pull it, while the magnets behind push it. The train glides forward without an engine on board.

One maglev line runs in Shanghai, China. Since 2004, it has carried passengers about 30 kilometers from the airport to the city at more than 400 kilometers an hour. The trip takes only about 8 minutes.

In 2015, a test train in Japan reached 603 kilometers an hour, a world record for trains.

But maglev trains cost a lot to build. They need their own guideway and cannot share ordinary rails.

In Saudi Arabia, a high-speed train links Makkah and Madinah, but it still runs on wheels. Someday, people may ride trains that float.

versions.title: Maglev Trains: Riding on Magnets
versions.text:
Imagine a train that hovers above the ground as it races across the countryside. It sounds like science fiction, but it is entirely real. These vehicles are called maglev trains, a name that is short for "magnetic levitation," which means rising into the air without any visible support.

A maglev train has no wheels touching its track. Instead, it floats between one and ten centimeters above a specially designed track called a guideway, supported entirely by powerful magnets.

Anyone who has experimented with two magnets understands the basic principle. Held one way, they attract each other; turned around, they push apart. A maglev train exploits this repelling force to lift itself off the guideway, and some designs use superconductors, which are materials cooled to extremely low temperatures so that they can create exceptionally strong magnetic fields.

On a conventional train, metal wheels roll against metal rails. The rubbing between them is called friction, and it slows the train, generates noise, and gradually wears out the equipment. Because a maglev train never touches the guideway, there is virtually no friction from the track, so it can travel at tremendous speeds while giving passengers a quiet, smooth ride. Air resistance, however, still pushes against the train, which is why maglevs have long, streamlined noses.

Magnets in the guideway also provide propulsion. They switch on and off in a carefully timed pattern, so the magnets ahead of the train pull it while the magnets behind push it. The train glides forward without an engine on board.

One maglev line operates in Shanghai, China. Since 2004, it has carried passengers about 30 kilometers from the airport to the city at more than 400 kilometers an hour, completing the journey in only about 8 minutes.

In 2015, an experimental train in Japan reached 603 kilometers an hour, establishing a world record for trains. Japan is now building a maglev line between Tokyo and Nagoya, and because the route must be as straight as possible, much of it runs through tunnels deep beneath the mountains.

However, maglev systems are extremely expensive to construct, and they require their own guideway because they cannot share ordinary railway tracks.

In Saudi Arabia, a high-speed railway connects Makkah and Madinah, but its trains still run on wheels. Someday, passengers may travel on trains that float.

HIGH.prompt: Do you think more countries should build maglev lines? Explain your opinion using both the advantages and the challenges described in the article.
checklist: I explained at least one advantage and one challenge of maglevs.
I supported my reasons with evidence from the article.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I think more countries should build maglev lines, because the advantages are impressive even though the challenges are real. Since maglev trains use levitation to float above the guideway, they have almost no friction from the track, which lets them travel extremely fast and quietly, as shown by the Shanghai maglev carrying passengers at over 400 kilometers an hour and a Japanese test train that set a world record of 603 kilometers an hour. The main challenge is that maglev propulsion needs its own expensive guideway built from scratch, since the trains cannot share ordinary rails like the Makkah-Madinah line does. Still, I believe the speed and comfort maglev trains offer make the investment in a dedicated guideway worthwhile for busy routes.
